claims.text: The as-cast MgAlCuZnGd alloy is in a non-equilibrium state.
The MgAlCuZnGd alloy has a density below 6 g/cm3.
The initial alloy contains a supersaturated solid solution together with early intermetallic formation.
Cyclic exposure at 700–900 °C produces differential oxidation kinetics in MgAlCuZnGd.
Mg oxidizes more rapidly and preferentially than the other constituents during the thermal cycles.
Preferential Mg oxidation promotes nucleation and growth of intermetallic phases at the surface.
Cyclic oxidation creates a coherent bilayer composed of an intermetallic/oxide-rich outer region and a less-transformed metastable interior.
The intermetallic/oxide surface layer acts as a diffusion barrier to corrosive species.
The intermetallic/oxide surface layer restricts oxygen penetration into the bulk.
Formation of the surface barrier slows subsequent oxidation-scale growth.
Formation of the surface barrier lowers corrosion current density relative to the untreated as-cast alloy.
Intermetallic phases can stabilize an Mg-containing matrix and impede propagation of corrosion fronts.
A rapidly solidified non-equilibrium cast microstructure can undergo significant evolution during subsequent high-temperature treatment.
The specified cyclic treatment can promote interfacial-layer development without allowing complete microstructural equilibration.
The untreated as-cast baseline lacks a coherent protective surface layer.
In situ high-temperature SEM and XPS can confirm the proposed stepwise evolution of the protective bilayer.
Failure to form the bilayer or failure to improve either oxidation or corrosion behavior would falsify the hypothesis.
The formal falsification rule requires both failure of bilayer formation and absence of statistically significant oxidation and corrosion improvements.

contradictions.description: The predicted-outcome field uses an OR criterion: either absence of the bilayer or unchanged performance would falsify the hypothesis. The formal falsification rule instead uses an AND criterion requiring both absence of the bilayer and no performance improvement.
